title: The Uncertainty Seminar: Evaluating Public Claims
instructions: 阅读以下模拟教育材料（非官方雅思测试）。先通读文章，理解大意；再完成10道题（单选、填空、判断正误/未提及）。填空题答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。注意：本材料为原创模拟内容，不涉及真实研究或引用。
passage:
A seminar on uncertainty in public claims was held last week at a community learning centre. The event was organised by a local group called Clear Thinking and was attended by about forty adults. The seminar was designed to help people evaluate claims they see in news reports, advertisements, and social media. The main speaker was Dr. Elena Marsh, a science communicator who has worked with several public health campaigns. The seminar was divided into three parts: a presentation, a group exercise, and a final discussion.

In the first part, Dr. Marsh explained why uncertainty is often hidden in public messages. She said that many claims are presented as certain when they are actually based on limited evidence. For example, a food product might be advertised as “proven to improve memory,” but the study behind it might have involved only twenty people. Dr. Marsh emphasised that the size of a study matters, and so does the way it was conducted. She also introduced the idea of “confidence levels,” which show how sure researchers are about their results. A confidence level of 95% does not mean there is a 95% chance the claim is true; it means that if the study were repeated many times, 95% of the results would fall within a certain range. This distinction was new to most participants. Dr. Marsh added that uncertainty is not a sign of bad science; rather, it is an honest reflection of what research can and cannot tell us. She noted that public messages often remove uncertainty to make claims sound more convincing, which can mislead people. For instance, advertisers may highlight a single positive result while ignoring the broader context of the research. This selective presentation can create a false sense of certainty and lead consumers to make poorly informed decisions. To illustrate further, she mentioned that even well-designed studies can have limitations, such as small sample sizes or confounding factors, and that acknowledging these limitations is part of responsible reporting. She explained that confounding factors are additional influences that researchers may not have controlled, and these can distort the apparent link between cause and effect. Recognising such details helps readers judge whether a claim is as strong as it first appears.

After the presentation, the participants were given a group exercise. They were divided into small groups and each group was given a short news article to analyse. The articles had been chosen to include different types of uncertainty. One group was asked to identify the source of a claim about a new diet. Another group had to find out whether a statistic about crime rates was based on a national survey or a local one. A third group was asked to check if a claim about a medicine had been approved by a regulatory agency. The groups were told to mark any sentences where uncertainty was not clearly stated. After twenty minutes, each group presented its findings. Many participants said they had not noticed the missing uncertainty before the exercise. The exercise helped them see how easily uncertainty can be overlooked when reading quickly. It also demonstrated that even seemingly straightforward articles can contain hidden assumptions or gaps in evidence.

In the final discussion, Dr. Marsh answered questions from the audience. One participant asked how ordinary people can check claims without special knowledge. Dr. Marsh suggested three simple steps: first, look for the original source of the claim; second, check whether the source is independent; and third, see if other reliable sources report the same thing. She warned that headlines are often written to attract attention, so they may exaggerate or simplify the findings. Another participant asked about the role of social media algorithms. Dr. Marsh explained that algorithms are designed to show content that keeps people engaged, which can mean that uncertain claims are repeated more often than careful corrections. She recommended that people follow a variety of sources and be cautious of claims that promise quick fixes. She also advised checking the date of the information, as old studies may no longer be relevant. In addition, she pointed out that algorithms can create echo chambers, where users mainly see information that confirms their existing beliefs, making it harder to encounter balanced perspectives. She suggested that users actively seek out opposing viewpoints and verify information through fact-checking websites. She added that this habit of checking several sources takes little time once it becomes routine, and it can greatly reduce the chance of being misled by a single dramatic headline.

The seminar ended with a short evaluation form. Participants were asked to rate the usefulness of the session and to suggest topics for future events. Most feedback was positive, and several people requested a follow-up seminar on how to read scientific studies. Clear Thinking plans to run a similar event next month, focusing on claims about climate and health. The organisers said that the seminar would be repeated in a larger venue because demand had been higher than expected. They also noted that the materials used in the exercise would be made available online after the event.

grammar.title: 被动语态、顺序、地点、变化及句子间衔接
grammar.explanation: 本课重点：1) 被动语态（be + 过去分词）用于强调动作承受者或未知执行者，如“The seminar was organised by a local group.”；2) 顺序（first, second, third）用于列举步骤；3) 地点介词（at, in, on）表示位置；4) 变化动词（become, increase, decrease）描述趋势；5) 句子间衔接词（however, therefore, for example）使逻辑清晰。注意区分新学形式（被动语态）与复习内容（顺序词）。
grammar.example: The event was organised by a local group called Clear Thinking.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: The new policy ______ by the committee last week.
questions.explanation: 被动语态结构为be + 过去分词，且时间状语last week表示过去，因此用was approved。
questions.evidence: The event was organised by a local group called Clear Thinking.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct word to show sequence: ______, you should check the source; second, check if it is independent.
questions.explanation: 列举步骤时用First, second, third等顺序词，此处与second对应，因此选First。
questions.evidence: first, look for the original source of the claim; second, check whether the source is independent

questions.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The meeting was held ______ a small room.
questions.explanation: 表示在某个空间内部用介词in，如in a room。
questions.evidence: A seminar on uncertainty in public claims was held last week at a community learning centre.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct verb to show change: The number of participants ______ from 20 to 40.
questions.explanation: 从20到40是数量增加，因此用increased。
questions.evidence: demand had been higher than expected

questions.prompt: Choose the correct linking word: The study was small; ______, the results may not be reliable.
questions.explanation: 前后句为因果关系，因此用therefore表示“因此”。
questions.evidence: the size of a study matters

questions.prompt: Choose the correct passive form: The materials ______ online after the event.
questions.explanation: 被动语态将来时结构为will be + 过去分词，因此选will be made available。
questions.evidence: the materials used in the exercise would be made available online after the event

questions.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: The seminar ended ______ a short evaluation form.
questions.explanation: end with表示“以……结束”，因此选with。
questions.evidence: The seminar ended with a short evaluation form.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct linking word: Headlines are often written to attract attention; ______, they may exaggerate the findings.
questions.explanation: 前后为因果关系，因此用as a result表示“结果”。
questions.evidence: headlines are often written to attract attention, so they may exaggerate or simplify the findings
